newsitem.title: UK: Ffr tiptoes up in Europe but shaky on poll nerves.
newsitem.headline: Ffr tiptoes up in Europe but shaky on poll nerves.

text.p: The French franc retrieved some of Monday's losses from a broadly steady mark in morning Europe after expectations of early elections in France were confirmed.

But though opinion polls suggest the centre-right will retain power in the poll on May 25 and June 1, analysts said market fear of a Socialist win and potentially less pro-EMU government would keep the franc under pressure for now.

"The mark's going to continue to receive support from ongoing political uncertainty in France, but unless the Socialists win there's not going to be a change in policy," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London.
In a TV address on Monday night, Chirac said he had brought forward the poll so the French could "express themselves clearly on the scale and speed of change over the next five years".
French participation in the European single currency was essential, Chirac said. The opposition Socialists accused the government of planning tough new austerity measures.

"The French election looks like it's turning into a second referendum. It will be test of France's fiscal resolve and there is some risk to the EMU project," said Thomas Rayner, international economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull here.
The franc was quoted at 3.3732/35 per mark by 0806 GMT, up from late Monday's European level of 3.3769/71. It remained weaker than last week's range of 3.3615 to 3.3698.

The lira, infected yesterday with the franc's malaise, also steadied but remained shaky. Analysts said the EMU jitters stirred by the French election and doubts over Italy's planned mini-budget would continue to plague the Italian currency.

Data from six Italian cities on Monday, indicating a preliminary April CPI rate of 1.8 percent year-on-year, were seen opening the door to an interest rate cut. But analysts warned that lira difficulties could bar that door for now.
"Italy desperately needs to cut interest rates, but the weakness of the lira may delay the much-needed easing," said DKB's Stamenkovic.
Five more Italian cities release their data at 1530 GMT.
The lira stood at 994.55/85 per mark at 0825 GMT compared to late Monday's European level of 995.00/50.

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer offered further support to a mark already benefiting from EMU worries, analysts said. Tietmeyer told a banking audience on Monday that a delay to currency union could be considered if big countries failed to meet the entry criteria.
But traders said the market impact was tempered by Tietmeyer's comment that the Bundesbank was working on the assumption that the euro would be launched on schedule in 1999.

Buba vice-president Johann-Wilhelm Gaddum said there was no problem in beginning EMU with a smaller group, while the International Monetary Fund warned that Germany, France and Italy should do more to cut their deficits for monetary union.

Germany's six top economic research institutes released their spring report, predicting the country's 1997 budget deficit at 3.0 to 3.2 percent of GDP, falling to 2.9 percent in 1998. The EMU target deficit/GDP ratio is 3.0 percent.
They estimated German GDP growth at 2.25 percent this year and 2.75 the next, with 1997 jobless seen at 4.28 million and 1998 at 4.16 million. The figures were leaked yesterday.
The institutes predicted the Bundesbank would leave interest rates steady in 1997, unless the dollar climbed sharply, but saw a small tightening early next year.

Meanwhile, Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler said he saw no reason for upturn in German rates in the foreseeable future, and said the outlook was favourable for Germany to post growth of about 2.5 percent in 1997.

With the market awaiting this weekend's G7 meeting to hear what the major industrial nations will say about forex levels, Zeitler said the necessity for major currencies to correct against the mark was now over.
However, the German institutes predicted the dollar -- currently trading around 1.70-71 marks -- would average 1.80 marks in 1998.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
